liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini, Virgin (United States)
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Do not turn back
theme: Receive the good things of daily life without forgetting the Lord who will come.
introduction: Jesus recalls Noah and Lot, then warns his disciples against turning back for what they have left behind. The Fathers do not hear a condemnation of marriage, meals, or honest work. They warn against an attachment to these things that makes us forget God's judgment. Augustine reads Lot's wife as a warning to keep our hope in God's promise when trouble comes.
hero_alt: Jesus teaches his disciples beneath gold mosaic arches, with Noah's ark on blue waters and a distant burning city in separate background scenes.
closing: Lot's wife becomes, in Augustine's reading, a warning against turning from the hope of God's promise in a time of trouble. The disciples' final question draws their attention to Christ himself. Cyril pictures the saints hastening to meet the Son of Man when he comes.
copyright_notes: Scripture is an original modernization of the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, not of the USCCB or Vatican News Lectionary text. The complete Douay-Rheims passage Luke 17:26–37 is included, preserving its verse boundaries and textual form. The official sources establish the date and citation only. Patristic insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Comments on an immediate unit are attached to the verse they illuminate.
verse_numbering_note: The Douay-Rheims source includes both the women grinding and the men in the field in verse 35, the disciples' question in verse 36, and Jesus' answer in verse 37. The Catena's printed Gospel places the men in the field in verse 36 and combines the question and answer in verse 37. The modern official Lectionary omits the men-in-the-field sentence. This edition preserves the complete public-domain Douay-Rheims text and numbering rather than harmonizing those textual forms.

verses.text: As it came to pass in the days of Noah, so will it also be in the days of the Son of man.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede connects Noah's days with the lightning Jesus has just described. Both images warn of a coming that will be sudden.
verses.commentary: Bede reads this comparison in the light of Jesus' preceding words about lightning. The Lord has already described the swiftness of his coming; now the days of Noah and Lot give that warning a place in human history. In both cases destruction came suddenly upon people who were continuing their ordinary lives. Bede later connects the warning with forgetfulness of God's judgment. The Judge who now sees everything without being seen will appear to judge everything. The comparison calls attention to that coming before it arrives.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:26–30

verses.text: They ate and drank, married wives, and were given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Marriage, food, and drink are not condemned. Ambrose says these sustain human life; the warning concerns sin and the loss of moderation.
verses.commentary: Ambrose insists that the flood must be understood in relation to human sin. God did not create evil; people brought its consequences upon themselves through what they deserved. Yet the mention of marriage, eating, and drinking must not be mistaken for a condemnation of these things. Marriage sustains the succession of human generations, while food and drink sustain our nature. Ambrose therefore asks for moderation in their use. His reading preserves their goodness while taking seriously the sins that brought judgment upon Noah's generation.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:26–30

verses.text: Likewise, as it came to pass in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Jesus names ordinary activities rather than Sodom's notorious sins. Bede hears a warning about lawful pleasures taken to excess.
verses.commentary: Bede notices what Jesus leaves unmentioned. Instead of naming the terrible wickedness associated with Sodom, he lists activities that might seem slight faults or no faults at all. People eat, trade, plant, and build. Bede reads this choice as a warning about excess even in lawful pleasures. If such pleasures, when abused, receive so fearful a judgment, the punishment of unlawful pleasures must be taken seriously. The ordinary appearance of the activities does not remove the need for moderation or the reality of God's judgment.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:26–30

verses.text: On the day Lot went out of Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all.
verses.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
verses.insight: Eusebius notices the order: Lot leaves before the fire falls, as Noah enters the ark before the flood. He relates this to the separation of the just from the wicked.
verses.commentary: Eusebius pays attention to the timing of the judgment. Fire does not fall upon Sodom before Lot has gone out, just as the flood does not overwhelm the earth before Noah has entered the ark. While these righteous men remain among the wicked, God holds back his anger so that they will not perish with the sinners. When judgment comes, he withdraws the righteous. Eusebius applies this pattern to the end of the world: the consummation will not come before the just have been separated from the wicked.
verses.source_label: Eusebius of Caesarea, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:26–30

verses.text: So will it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: The Lord who sees all things unseen will appear to judge all things. Bede warns against becoming so bound to this world that we forget his judgment.
verses.commentary: Bede contrasts the Lord's present hiddenness with his future appearance. We do not yet see him, but nothing is hidden from his sight. When he appears, the one who has always seen all things will judge all things. Bede connects the time of that coming with people who have forgotten his judgments and become enslaved to the world. The examples of Noah and Lot thus prepare for this declaration about the Son of Man. His revelation will interrupt a world that has ceased to attend to him.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:26–30

verses.text: In that hour, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not go down to take them away; and likewise, let the one who is in the field not turn back.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine reads the housetop as the freedom of spiritual life. Trouble must not draw us back into the worldly attachments we have renounced.
verses.commentary: Augustine gives the housetop a spiritual meaning. The person who has left carnal things behind breathes the free air of a spiritual life. Descending for the household vessels becomes an image of returning, under pressure, to a life governed by bodily pleasure. He also reads the field as the work of the Church, recalling Paul planting and Apollos watering. Those engaged in that labour must not turn back toward the worldly prospects they have renounced. Both images warn against surrendering spiritual progress in a time of tribulation.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:31–33

verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Lot's wife warns those who turn away from hope when trouble comes. Augustine sees her pillar of salt as a warning meant to preserve the hearts of others.
verses.commentary: Augustine reads Lot's wife as a figure of people who look back in a time of trouble and turn aside from the hope of God's promise. Her fate therefore speaks to those who have already begun to leave danger behind but are tempted to reverse their course. The pillar of salt is itself a warning against repeating her choice. Augustine also draws on salt's preserving quality: her example should season the hearts of those who remember her, so that they do not become corrupt through the same backward turn.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:31–33

verses.text: Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it; and whoever loses it will preserve it.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril explains this loss through St Paul's words about crucifying the flesh with its passions and desires. It calls for perseverance and devotion in the struggle.
verses.commentary: Cyril asks how someone can lose his own life in order to save it. He answers by turning to St Paul's account of those who have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. This gives the saying a concrete spiritual meaning: a person perseveres with devotion in the conflict against those passions. The loss Christ speaks of is understood through that crucifixion of the flesh. Cyril's explanation directs the hearer toward faithful struggle rather than allowing the apparent contradiction of losing and saving to remain unexplained.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:31–33

verses.text: I say to you: in that night there will be two men in one bed; one will be taken and the other left.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril sees the bed as an image of the ease wealth can bring. Yet wealth alone does not decide the outcome: not all the rich are wicked.
verses.commentary: Cyril understands the two men resting in one bed as an image of the rich who repose in worldly pleasures. A bed signifies rest. But he immediately refuses to identify everyone who possesses wealth with wickedness. One may be good and elect in faith, and so be taken, while another is left. Cyril relates this distinction to Christ's descent for judgment. The angels bring the holy and righteous to meet him, while others remain for punishment. Shared outward comfort does not make the two men's spiritual condition the same.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:34–37

verses.text: Two women will be grinding together: one will be taken and the other left. Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine sees different forms of life within the Church in the bed, mill, and field. In each, some remain faithful and others fall away.
verses.commentary: Augustine reads the three scenes as three classes of people. The bed signifies those who prefer a quiet life, apart from secular and ecclesiastical business. Those grinding represent people under teachers whose temporal activities serve the Church. The field signifies those who labour in the Church's ministry. Each class contains two sorts of people: some remain in the Church and are taken, while others fall away and are left. In this reading, sharing a form of life or a sphere of work does not settle whether a person will persevere.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:34–37 (including both mill and field)

verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril calls the disciples' question useful. The Lord's answer points them toward the gathering of the saints to the Son of Man.
verses.commentary: Cyril says the disciples do not ask their question without purpose. Jesus has spoken of some being taken, and they want to know where. Cyril follows their question into the answer about the body and the eagles. As birds that feed on flesh gather wherever a body lies, so the saints will hasten to meet the Son of Man when he comes. The question leads, in Cyril's reading, from the separation Jesus has announced to the gathering of the holy around him at his coming.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:34–37 (question numbered 17:36 in Douay-Rheims)

verses.text: He said to them: Wherever the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered together.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose likens the righteous to eagles that soar above earthly things. He directs their gathering toward Christ's body, recalling the women and Apostles at his tomb.
verses.commentary: Ambrose compares righteous souls to eagles because they rise high and leave lower things behind. To understand the body, he recalls Joseph receiving Jesus' body from Pilate and the women and Apostles gathered around the Lord's tomb. He then looks ahead to Christ's coming in the clouds, when every eye will see him. His reading also recalls Christ's flesh as true food and the Church as his body. Around this body gather those who believe in the Incarnation and fly on the wings of the Spirit.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 17:34–37
